crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
children.blurb: Pathology detection and scan triage covers software that reads medical images to find signs of disease and software that decides which studies a radiologist should read first.

children.name: Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans
children.blurb: Synthetic imaging from existing scans is the practice of generating new medical images, such as CT, MRI or X-ray views, from scans that already exist rather than acquiring new ones from a patient.

children.name: Anatomical Models and 3D Printing
children.blurb: Anatomical models and 3D printing in radiology covers the conversion of CT, MRI and ultrasound volumes into physical objects: patient-specific replicas of bones, vessels, organs and tumours, plus surgical guides, implants and prosthetics.

children.name: Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement
children.blurb: Point of care ultrasound enhancement covers the software that cleans up, interprets, or extends the images a clinician captures at the bedside with a handheld or cart based probe.

children.name: Radiomics
children.blurb: Radiomics is the extraction of large numbers of quantitative features from medical images, most often CT, MRI and PET scans, and the use of those features to build models that describe a tumour or tissue beyond what the eye can see.

sections.body: Diagnostic imaging is where artificial intelligence has moved furthest from research papers into daily clinical work. Software reads chest X-rays, mammograms, CT scans and MRI studies, flags possible abnormalities and sorts the queue so the most urgent cases reach a radiologist first. Some systems draft a preliminary report or highlight a region of interest, while others work behind the scenes on image quality, noise reduction and reconstruction. Synthetic imaging takes an existing scan and generates a new view of the same anatomy, for example a CT-like image from an MRI, to spare a patient a second procedure. Radiomics goes further and turns the texture and shape of a lesion into numerical features that can be fed to a model. None of this replaces the radiologist, and the field is best understood as a set of tools that change what a human reviewer sees and when.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Detection and triage are the most mature parts, with several systems cleared by regulators for specific tasks such as spotting lung nodules or breast lesions. The hard problems are not the algorithms but the workflow, the variation between scanners and hospitals, and the fact that a model trained on one population often performs worse on another. Synthetic imaging is promising but still judged on whether it preserves the clinical detail a radiologist needs, and a generated image can look convincing while being wrong. Anatomical models and 3D printing are used in surgical planning, yet turning a scan into a printable model still involves manual segmentation for many cases. Ultrasound enhancement is difficult because of speckle and operator dependence, and radiomics has struggled to move from promising studies to routine use because features are sensitive to how the scan was acquired. The honest limit across all of it is that most systems are narrow, validated on particular tasks and populations, and need a human to confirm the finding.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the path of an image from acquisition to decision. Pathology Detection and Scan Triage is the entry point for readers who want to know how a model finds a lesion and how that finding changes the order in which cases are read. Synthetic Imaging from Existing Scans covers what happens when one modality is used to estimate another, and why that is useful and risky. Anatomical Models and 3D Printing sits at the boundary between image and physical object, for readers interested in surgical planning and the segmentation work it requires. Point of Care Ultrasound Enhancement addresses the hardest imaging setting, where the operator, the machine and the moment all vary. Radiomics is the most quantitative page, for readers who want to know how image data becomes features and why reproducibility is the central difficulty. Read together, they show a field that is strong on narrow detection tasks and still working out how to make its outputs reliable across hospitals, machines and patients.
